title: Design a chat system like WhatsApp or Slack.
description: Real-time messaging system with 1:1 and group chats, message persistence, and read receipts.

data.text: **Question:** Design a chat system like WhatsApp or Slack.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: Real-time message delivery with low latency

data.text: The system uses WebSockets for real-time communication. A load balancer distributes connections across stateless chat servers. Messages are stored in a distributed database (Cassandra or DynamoDB) for persistence. A message queue handles async processing for notifications and media uploads. Redis caches active user sessions and recent messages.

data.title: Message Ordering
data.text: Use Lamport timestamps or logical clocks combined with server-side sequencing to maintain message order across multiple chat servers.

data.title: Horizontal and Vertical Scaling
items: Partition conversations by conversation_id for sharding
Use separate read replicas for message history queries
Cache active conversations and last 100 messages per user
Offload media processing to background workers via message queue
Use CDN for static media assets

data.title: Message Persistence
data.text: Avoid losing messages during failover by writing to a write-ahead log (WAL) before acknowledging delivery to the sender.

cards.title: WebSockets vs Long Polling
cards.description: WebSockets provide lower latency but require persistent connections. Long polling is simpler but has higher overhead.

cards.title: Push vs Pull for Notifications
cards.description: Push notifications via APNs/FCM are real-time but depend on third-party services. Pull is more reliable but uses more battery.

items.question: How do you handle offline users?
items.answer: Messages for offline users are stored in the database and pushed via notification when they reconnect. The client syncs missed messages on reconnection.

items.question: How do you ensure message delivery?
items.answer: Use acknowledgments at multiple levels: sender to server, server to recipient, and optional end-to-end encryption verification.

items.question: How do you handle group chats with thousands of members?
items.answer: Use fanout services that replicate messages to member shards asynchronously. Limit fanout concurrency and cache group membership.

items.question: What database should I use for messages?
items.answer: Cassandra or DynamoDB work well for high-write, time-series message data. Use composite keys (conversation_id + timestamp) for range queries.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use WebSockets for real-time bidirectional communication
Cache active sessions and recent messages for low latency
Use message queues for async processing of media and notifications
Lamport timestamps maintain ordering across distributed servers
data.takeaway: Chat systems need low-latency delivery, horizontal scalability through sharding, and careful handling of offline and high-member scenarios.
